379.title: The golden calf (Exodus 32)
379.hook: they melt their earrings into a god they can see
379.howItsDone: The Catechism teaches that idolatry includes putting power, pleasure, money or any created thing in God's place, and that venerating holy images is not idolatry, because the honor passes to the person the image represents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Decalogue, which opens with a rescue, not a rule. Your line was freedom first, then the law.

Moses has been up the mountain for forty days. No word, just a cloud on the summit and silence. Down in the camp, people start talking. Maybe he's dead. And the God he talks to is invisible, up there in the smoke. So they go to Aaron, Moses's brother, the one left in charge: make us gods to go before us. As for this Moses, we don't know what happened to him. And Aaron says: bring me your gold earrings.
screen: `FORTY DAYS. NO MOSES.` → `MAKE US GODS.` → `BRING ME YOUR EARRINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the calf. Aaron melts the gold and shapes a young bull, and the people say, "These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt." Then Aaron builds an altar and announces a feast of the Lord, using God's own name. That's the twist. They aren't exactly walking away from the God who rescued them. They're trying to make that God visible, portable, controllable. Second, the excuse. When Moses comes down, sees the dancing and smashes the tablets, Aaron says, more or less: they gave me gold, I threw it in the fire, and out came this calf. It's what a parent might hear from a child standing next to a broken vase. Third, the word. Idol comes from the Greek eidolon, an image, even a phantom: something that looks like the real thing and isn't. The Catechism widens it. Idolatry isn't only about statues: a person commits idolatry whenever they honor a created thing in place of God, and it lists power, pleasure, money, race, the state. Fourth, the obvious question. Catholic churches are full of statues and icons. Are those idols? The Catholic and Orthodox answer comes from a council at Nicaea in 787: the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows. In Catholic teaching, the prayer goes to the person, not the plaster. Some Protestant churches, reading the same commandment, keep their walls plain. The real test in Exodus 32 isn't whether there's gold in the room. It's what the people let take God's place.
screen: `THESE ARE THY GODS, O ISRAEL.` · `THIS CALF CAME OUT.` · `EIDOLON: AN IMAGE, A PHANTOM.` · `WHAT TAKES GOD'S PLACE?`

segments.voice: Ask yourself honestly: what do I check first in the morning, what do I most fear losing, where does my money go when it's tight? Some answers will be good things, work, family, health, and the calf was made of good gold, too; just notice which one sits in the center, and whether that's where you want it. If you pray, set that thing before God and ask for the right order; if not, simply hold the question.
Idol. From Greek eidolon, an image. Anything, golden or not, that a person lets take the place of God. Today's word.
Your line: what are you worshiping. Good things can still sit in the wrong place. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

380.title: God's back (Exodus 33:18–23)
380.hook: Moses hidden in a cleft of rock sees God pass by
380.howItsDone: Some Catholics pray the examen at night, looking back over the day to notice where God was present, a practice taught by Saint Ignatius of Loyola, and the Church teaches that seeing God face to face is the joy of heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden calf, and the question of an idol: what takes God's place? Your line was what are you worshiping.

After the calf and the broken tablets, Moses makes one more request, and it's a bold one. He has spoken with God in the cloud and heard the voice. Now he asks in four words, as the Douay-Rheims has it: "Shew me thy glory." Not a sign, not a plan, not help with the people. Just: let me see you. And God says yes, and also no.
screen: `AFTER THE CALF, ONE MORE REQUEST.` → `SHEW ME THY GLORY.` → `YES, AND ALSO NO.`

segments.voice: First, the yes. God says: I'll make all my goodness pass before you, and I'll call out my name. Second, the no. "Thou canst not see my face: for man shall not see me and live." Here's the strange part. Earlier in this same chapter, the text says God spoke to Moses face to face, the way a man speaks to his friend. So which is it? The Bible holds both: real closeness, real conversation, and still a limit. Third, the rock. God says: stand on the rock by me. When my glory passes, I'll put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I've gone by. Then I'll take my hand away, "and thou shalt see my back parts: but my face thou canst not see." The Hebrew word is achorai, my back, what's behind me, after me. Moses sees God only from behind, only as God is going past. Fourth, what Catholic writers made of it. Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Moses, said that seeing God's back means following him: you see the back of someone you walk behind. Some readers find a version of this in their own lives: they rarely notice grace in the moment, and see its shape only afterward, looking back. The Church teaches that seeing God face to face is the promise of heaven. Paul says it in a line: we see now through a glass in a dark manner, but then face to face. And centuries later, on another mountain, the Gospels put Moses beside Jesus at the Transfiguration, looking at a face that shines like the sun.
screen: `SHEW ME THY GLORY.` · `NO ONE SEES MY FACE AND LIVES.` · `A CLEFT IN THE ROCK, A HAND.` · `ACHORAI: SEEN FROM BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Pick one hard stretch of your life that's over now, or mostly over, and walk back through it slowly, without reliving it: who showed up that you didn't expect, what door opened, what small mercy did you barely notice at the time? If you pray, thank God for one thing you only see now; if not, simply name what carried you.

Your line: seen from behind. Some things are clearest once they've passed. See you tomorrow.

381.title: The dwelling (Exodus 35–40)
381.hook: everyone brings something, and the cloud fills the tent
381.howItsDone: In Catholic churches the Eucharist is reserved in a tabernacle, named after the tent in Exodus, with a lamp kept burning beside it, and parishes rely on volunteers' skills, from musicians and sacristans to cooks and catechists.

segments.voice: Yesterday, God's back: Moses in the cleft of the rock, seeing the glory only as it passed. Your line was seen from behind.

Here's a sentence you'll almost never hear in a parish bulletin: please stop giving, we have too much. It's in Exodus. Moses asks for materials for a tent where God will dwell among the people, and only from those whose hearts move them to give. They come morning after morning with gold jewelry, colored yarn, goat hair, wood, oil and spices, until the craftsmen tell Moses the people are bringing much more than they need. So Moses sends word through the camp: nobody make anything else for the sanctuary. The people had to be held back from giving.
screen: `FOR WHOEVER'S HEART IS MOVED.` → `MORNING AFTER MORNING.` → `PLEASE STOP. WE HAVE TOO MUCH.`

segments.voice: First, the gifts. The last six chapters of Exodus read like a building inventory, and that's the point: everyone's in it. Rulers bring precious stones. Skilled women spin blue, purple and scarlet yarn with their own hands, and some spin goat hair. Others bring their bronze mirrors, which are melted down for the great washbasin. Nobody's gift is too ordinary. Second, the artist. God calls a craftsman named Bezalel and fills him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, understanding and skill, to work gold, cut stones, carve wood. What the Spirit gives him, the text says, is skill with his hands. A partner named Oholiab works with him, and they teach others. Third, the dwelling. In Hebrew it's the mishkan, from a verb that means to dwell or to settle. It's a tent, made to be taken down and carried. When it's set up, the cloud covers it, and the glory of the Lord fills it so completely that Moses himself can't go in. The God of the burning mountain now lives in a tent in the middle of the camp. Fourth, where Catholics see it every Sunday. The place in a Catholic church where the Eucharist is kept is called the tabernacle, named for this tent, and for Catholics the lamp burning beside it says what the cloud said: God is here. John's Gospel uses the same picture: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. The Greek verb means, literally, he pitched his tent.

segments.voice: Bezalel brought his hands, the women their spinning, someone a mirror: what's yours? Maybe you cook, fix a sink, keep accounts, sing, drive, read aloud or set up chairs; picture one community you belong to, and the one place that gift would fit. If you pray, offer that skill to God; if not, simply notice that you have something to bring.
The dwelling. The tent built from everyone's gifts, where the cloud of God's glory came to live in the middle of the camp. Today's word.

382.title: Be holy (Leviticus 19)
382.hook: be holy, and thou shalt love thy friend as thyself, and leave gleanings for the poor
382.howItsDone: The Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium teaches the universal call to holiness, and many Catholic parishes run food pantries and collections for the poor; some Catholic groups also organize gleaning on farms after the harvest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dwelling, a tent built from everyone's gifts and filled with the cloud of glory. Your line was everyone brought something.

Leviticus has a reputation. It's where people who promise to read the whole Bible quietly give up: sacrifices, skin diseases, which animals you can eat. Then chapter nineteen opens with a command that sounds enormous: "Be ye holy, because I the Lord your God am holy." You'd expect what follows to be about the temple, or incense, or long prayers. Instead it's about farming, and wages, and how you treat a deaf man and a blind man. Holiness, it turns out, happens in a wheat field.
screen: `THE BOOK PEOPLE GIVE UP ON.` → `BE YE HOLY.` → `HOLINESS IN A WHEAT FIELD.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Holy, in Hebrew kadosh, means set apart, different, belonging to God. The plural, kedoshim, is how the chapter begins, and Jewish tradition still names this section of Leviticus by that word. Second, the corners. When you reap your field, God says, don't harvest all the way to the edges or go back for the stalks you dropped. Don't strip your vineyard bare or pick up the grapes that fell. Leave them for the poor and the stranger. The edges of your field aren't fully yours. Jewish law still keeps this as peah, the corner, with a whole section of the Mishnah devoted to it. Later in the Bible, a poor foreign widow named Ruth will survive by gathering exactly these leftovers. Third, the list. Pay your worker the same day. Don't curse the deaf, and don't put a stumbling block in front of the blind. Stand up for the old. Use honest weights in the market. Love the stranger as yourself, because you were strangers in Egypt. And in the middle of it all, the line Jesus will later call the second great commandment. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, says: "Thou shalt love thy friend as thyself." Most English Bibles say neighbor; the Hebrew word, rea, can mean either. Fourth, what the Church draws from it. The Second Vatican Council taught that every baptized person, not only priests and nuns, is called to holiness. Leviticus nineteen shows what that looks like at ground level: in the paycheck, the market, the harvest, and what you leave at the edges for someone else.
screen: `KADOSH: SET APART FOR GOD.` · `LEAVE THE CORNERS OF THE FIELD.` · `HONEST WAGES, HONEST WEIGHTS.` · `LOVE THY FRIEND AS THYSELF.`

segments.voice: Think about your own fields: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, the last slice of something, and find one corner you usually harvest right to the edge. Picture leaving it instead: a bag for the food pantry, a generous tip, ten minutes for someone else, the last good seat. If you pray, offer that corner to God; if not, simply picture who might find it.
Be holy. The command that opens Leviticus nineteen, lived out in fields, wages, and the corners left for the poor. Today's word.
Your line: leave the corners. What's left at the edges feeds someone else. That's day three hundred eighty-two.

383.title: Jubilee (Leviticus 25)
383.hook: every fiftieth year debts forgiven and land returned; the Church still keeps holy years
383.howItsDone: The Catholic Church proclaims ordinary jubilee years, when pilgrims pass through the holy doors of Rome's major basilicas and seek reconciliation, and popes have also called extraordinary jubilees, such as the Year of Mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, be holy: holiness in wheat fields, wages and the corners of a field. Your line was leave the corners.

In Philadelphia there's a cracked bell, the Liberty Bell, with a line of scripture around its top about proclaiming liberty throughout all the land. It's from Leviticus twenty-five. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, words it differently: "proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land." Liberty or remission, the verse wasn't first about a nation's independence. It was about a year. A strange, radical year that came around once every half century.
screen: `A CRACKED BELL IN PHILADELPHIA.` → `PROCLAIM LIBERTY.` → `ONCE EVERY HALF CENTURY.`

segments.voice: First, the count. Every seventh year in Israel was a sabbath for the land: no planting, the fields rest. Count seven of those, forty-nine years, and the fiftieth is the jubilee. It begins on the Day of Atonement with a blast on the ram's horn through the whole land. The year's Hebrew name, yovel, is traditionally linked to that ram's horn, and it's where the word jubilee comes from. Second, what happens. Land a family sold in hard times goes back to them. People who sold themselves into service for debt go free and return to their families. The land rests again. And God gives the reason: the land is mine, and you are strangers and guests with me. Third, the honest question. Did Israel ever fully keep it? The sources are mostly silent, and scholars still debate it. But the idea never went away. When Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, he read from Isaiah about the acceptable year of the Lord, and some readers hear in it the language of jubilee. Fourth, the Catholic holy year. In 1300, Pope Boniface the Eighth proclaimed the first Christian jubilee, a year of pilgrimage and forgiveness in Rome. The Church still keeps them, opening holy doors in Rome that stay sealed between jubilees. Before the year 2000, Pope John Paul the Second called for the debts of the poorest nations to be reduced or forgiven, a jubilee for whole countries. And some word historians think the Latin heard yovel alongside iubilare, to shout for joy, which may be why our word sounds like joy.
screen: `SEVEN SEVENS, THEN THE FIFTIETH.` · `YOVEL: THE RAM'S HORN SOUNDS.` · `LAND RETURNS, DEBTORS GO FREE.` · `HOLY YEARS AND HOLY DOORS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing someone owes you: twenty dollars never paid back, an apology you're still waiting for, a favor you keep score of. Picture writing it off, the horn sounding and the slate clearing; you don't have to tell them, you just stop collecting. If you pray, you can say the line from the Our Father as Matthew gives it: "forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors"; if not, picture the ledger closing.
Jubilee. From yovel, the ram's horn: the fiftieth year, when land returned and debtors went free. The Church still keeps holy years. Today's word.
Your line: a year to set free. Every fifty years, the count started over. Day three hundred eighty-three, in the books.

384.title: The blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
384.hook: the Lord bless thee and keep thee: the priestly blessing still used at Mass
384.howItsDone: The priestly blessing from Numbers 6 is read at Mass on January 1, the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, and some solemn blessings at the end of Mass use its words; some Catholic parents also trace a cross on their children's foreheads with a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jubilee: the ram's horn, the fiftieth year, land returned and debts set free. Your line was a year to set free.

Near the end of a Mass, the people stop speaking, and something is said over them. A hand goes up, and the room hears words it didn't earn and didn't ask for. In the book of Numbers, God gives Moses three short lines for exactly this. They aren't a prayer for the people to memorize and recite. They're a blessing, spoken over someone, by someone else. And on some Sundays, those three lines from the desert are still spoken over a Catholic congregation before it goes home.
screen: `NEAR THE END OF MASS.` → `SAID OVER, NOT SAID BY.` → `THREE LINES FROM THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: First, who gives it. God tells Moses to tell Aaron and his sons, the priests: this is how you shall bless the people. Then the words, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord bless thee, and keep thee. The Lord shew his face to thee, and have mercy on thee. The Lord turn his countenance to thee, and give thee peace." Second, its shape. In Hebrew, the first line has three words, the second five, the third seven. It grows like a wave building, from keeping you safe, to looking at you with mercy, to peace, shalom, a word that reaches past quiet toward wholeness. Third, the face. Two of the three lines are about God's face. To have someone's face shine on you, or turn toward you, is the picture of being seen with delight; a child looking for a parent in the crowd at a school play knows exactly what that means. At the end God says: so they shall put my name on the people, and I will bless them. The priests speak; God does the blessing. Fourth, where Catholics hear it. On the first of January, the feast of Mary, Mother of God, it's the first reading at Mass. One of the solemn blessings a priest may give at the end of Mass in Ordinary Time uses its words. Saint Francis of Assisi wrote it out by hand for his friend Brother Leo, and that parchment still survives in Assisi. And Jewish priests' descendants still give this blessing in synagogue, hands raised over the people.

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind, someone you love, someone struggling, maybe someone you find hard, and picture their face. Then, if you're comfortable, say the blessing over them, silently or aloud: the Lord bless thee, and keep thee; the Lord show his face to thee, and have mercy on thee; the Lord turn his countenance to thee, and give thee peace. If you don't pray, simply wish them those three things: safety, being seen with kindness, and peace.
The blessing. The priestly blessing of Numbers six: keeping, a shining face, mercy and peace. Still heard at Mass. Today's word.
Your line: the lord bless thee. Three lines, spoken over someone else. Until tomorrow.

385.title: The spies (Numbers 13–14)
385.hook: ten saw giants, two saw a land of milk and honey
385.howItsDone: The Catholic Church counts fortitude among the four cardinal virtues and among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit given in confirmation, and the Catechism describes it as firmness in difficulty that enables a person to conquer fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing: keeping, a shining face, mercy and peace. Your line was the lord bless thee. This week ran from the golden calf through God's back, the dwelling, be holy and the jubilee.

Twelve men come back from a forty-day scouting trip, and two of them carry a single cluster of grapes on a pole between them. That's how big the grapes are. They bring pomegranates and figs, too. The report starts well: it's a land flowing with milk and honey, just as promised. Then comes the word but. The people there are strong. The cities are great and walled. We saw giants, and next to them we were like grasshoppers, and that's how we looked to them.
screen: `TWELVE SCOUTS, FORTY DAYS.` → `GRAPES CARRIED ON A POLE.` → `BUT WE SAW GIANTS.`

segments.voice: First, two reports from one trip. All twelve saw the same fruit, the same walls, the same tall people. Ten came back saying we can't. Two, Caleb and Joshua, said we can. Caleb quiets the crowd: let's go up at once and take it, for we are well able. In Hebrew he doubles the verb, a way of insisting: we can, we surely can. Second, the grasshopper line. We were grasshoppers in our own sight, and so we were in theirs. How would they know what the giants thought? They never asked. They decided how small they were, and assumed everyone else agreed. Third, the night of weeping. The whole people cry all night. Let's choose a leader and go back to Egypt, they say, back to the bricks. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and plead: the land is very good; don't be afraid; the Lord is with us. And the crowd talks about stoning them. Fourth, the cost. A whole generation decides it can't, and the text takes them at their word: forty years in the wilderness, a year for each day of scouting, until that generation has passed, and of all those twenty and older who were counted, only Caleb and Joshua will walk into the land. The Church names this courage fortitude, one of the four cardinal virtues. The Catechism says it gives firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuing the good, and that it enables a person to conquer fear. Not to feel no fear. To conquer it.
screen: `SAME LAND, TWO REPORTS.` · `GRASSHOPPERS IN OUR OWN SIGHT.` · `A NIGHT OF WEEPING FOR EGYPT.` · `FORTITUDE: TO CONQUER FEAR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that feels like a giant right now, a deadline, a hard conversation, a health worry, and notice the story you're telling about yourself next to it. Then look at it the way Caleb did: same walls, same giants, but what's the fruit on the other side? If you pray, bring that fear to God and listen for Caleb's words; if not, just try on the second report.
The spies. Twelve scouts who saw the same land: ten saw giants and fear, two saw milk and honey and said we can. Today's word.
Your line: we are able. Ten saw giants; two saw the fruit. Day three hundred eighty-five.
